guidance.verdict: The classic first-year work — fixing bugs, writing small programs, trial runs, code comments — is the most handed-over set of rungs in this study.

project.title: Ship a small tool end to end, and own the 'why'
phases: Days 1–30: pick a real user (a club, a shop, your team). Write a one-page requirements and feasibility note before any code — what is in, what is out, what it costs.
Days 31–60: build it with AI doing the typing. Keep a decision log: each design choice, the alternatives, and why you chose. Review every AI diff as if you were the senior.
Days 61–90: put it in front of the user, run a status review with them, and write the post-mortem. The repo shows code; the log and post-mortem show judgement.

team: Stop measuring juniors on tickets closed. Bug-fix and maintenance tickets are where AI already does most of the work.
Give every junior one requirements conversation per sprint (task 21662, 'analyse user needs… feasibility'). It's a holding rung, so juniors can learn it with AI's help.
Make code review two-way: juniors review AI-generated diffs and explain them aloud. Validating output is the new apprenticeship.

roles.name: QA / test engineer
occupations: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers

guidance.verdict: Finding, documenting and first-pass debugging of defects — the entry door into QA — is mostly handed to AI now.

project.title: Become the person who decides what 'good enough to ship' means
phases: Days 1–30: take an open-source app; let AI generate the bug list. Then triage it yourself — severity, user impact, what was missed — and compare.
Days 31–60: write a release-readiness standard for that app: which risks block a launch, which do not, and why.
Days 61–90: send usability recommendations to the maintainers as a proper issue thread. Track what gets accepted.

team: Assume the defect-logging rung is gone. Juniors should start one rung up, on triage and impact calls, with a senior pairing.
Rotate juniors into design reviews early. Usability feedback to developers (task 14653) is still mostly done with AI rather than by it.
Score juniors on escaped defects and on how good their judgement was, not on bug counts.

guidance.verdict: Routine site updates have flipped to mostly AI-done; writing and maintaining site code is close behind (cracking, not yet broken).

project.title: Turn a vague brief into a spec, then into a site
phases: Days 1–30: interview a small business owner. Write the technical requirements (task 14702) and a sequence diagram of the key user flow.
Days 31–60: build with AI, but write the spec first and hold AI output to it. Document every place AI drifted from the spec.
Days 61–90: hand over with a site spec document a stranger could maintain. That document is the portfolio piece.

team: Hand update and maintenance tickets to AI-assisted pipelines, and move juniors to requirements and spec work sooner.
Pair each junior with a senior on one architecture choice per quarter, so 'select languages, tools' (14711) isn't learnt only by watching.
Make 'spec quality' a review criterion. It is the skill the data says still needs a person.

guidance.verdict: Answering user questions is the single biggest task in this study by Claude usage (2% of all Claude.ai usage that maps to an O*NET task), and two-thirds of it is now handed over.

project.title: Run a tiny IT evaluation like a consultant
phases: Days 1–30: shadow the help desk (or a family/hostel network). Log the top 20 problems and how often they recur.
Days 31–60: evaluate two tools that would remove the top 5 causes. Compare on cost, effort and risk (task 1292).
Days 61–90: write and present the recommendation. Then measure ticket volume afterwards.

team: Tier-1 answering is the rung most at risk. Redesign L1 roles around root-cause analysis and recommending fixes, not replying to tickets.
Give L1 staff ownership of the knowledge base the AI answers from. Curating the AI's sources is a real skill.
Create an explicit L1→L2 path that doesn't depend on years of ticket volume.

guidance.verdict: Dashboard upkeep is mostly handed over; cleaning data and standard reports are cracking. Synthesis and recommending action still hold.

project.title: One dataset, one decision, one recommendation
phases: Days 1–30: pick a public Indian dataset (e.g. data.gov.in) and a real decision someone faces. Let AI do the cleaning, and audit what it changed.
Days 31–60: find the drivers (task 21832) and test whether your model holds up (21837). Write down what would change your mind.
Days 61–90: deliver a one-page recommendation to a named audience (21836, a holding senior rung). Publish it with the notebook.

team: Stop hiring analysts to maintain dashboards; that rung is 89% automation in this data.
Every junior analysis should end in a 'so what' paragraph a manager can act on, and be reviewed on that paragraph.
Have juniors present to stakeholders early, with a senior in the room.

guidance.verdict: The support-desk side of the systems-analyst job (troubleshooting, helping users) is heavily handed over; the requirements and design work holds.

project.title: Map a real process and redesign it
phases: Days 1–30: pick a messy process (college admissions, a shop's ordering). Interview the people who run it and map it as-is.
Days 31–60: define the goals of the new system and draw the to-be flow (task 3476). Use AI to stress-test edge cases.
Days 61–90: write the requirements document plus a cost-benefit note. Walk the owner through it and record their objections.

team: Don't start juniors on L2 support as a rite of passage; that rung is mostly automated.
Put juniors in requirements workshops from month one, as note-taker first and then co-facilitator.
Use AI-drafted requirements as the starting point and grade juniors on what they catch.

guidance.verdict: The exception: no junior financial-analyst rung is mostly handed over. People mostly work through these tasks with AI rather than delegating them.

project.title: Cover one company like a sell-side analyst
phases: Days 1–30: pick one listed Indian company. Track its filings and news (task 21596), and keep a weekly log of what changed and why it matters.
Days 31–60: build a simple forecast model and write the investment case. Use AI to challenge your assumptions.
Days 61–90: publish the note with a clear call and the risks. Revisit it after the next results.

team: This is the role where junior work still builds judgement. Protect it, and don't automate it away for speed.
Use AI as a sparring partner in model reviews, not a replacement for the junior's first draft.
Watch the cracking rungs (reports on trends, interpreting risk data) and re-check them each data release.

guidance.verdict: Bookkeeping (ledger postings, classifying and recording entries) is where accounting's bottom rungs are breaking; analysis of the business still holds.

project.title: From entries to advice for one small business
phases: Days 1–30: take a small business's books (a family shop, a startup). Let AI categorise and post the entries, and check every exception.
Days 31–60: analyse costs, revenue trends and obligations (task 21519). Find three things the owner doesn't know.
Days 61–90: present a short advisory memo and a 6-month projection. Ask the owner what they will change.

team: Articleship and junior roles built on postings and reconciliations are on the rungs AI does most. Redesign them around exceptions and review.
Give juniors the 'why' questions: variance explanations, cost drivers, client queries.
Make reviewing AI-posted entries a formal, logged control. It's both a learning loop and an audit need.

roles.name: Digital marketer
occupations: Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists

guidance.verdict: The other exception: no junior marketing rung is yet mostly handed over, but web-metrics collection and reporting are cracking.

project.title: Run a measured campaign for a real cause
phases: Days 1–30: pick a small brand or NGO. Set up analytics, define 3 KPIs, and write why each matters.
Days 31–60: run two campaign variants. Let AI draft the content, and you design the test.
Days 61–90: forecast next quarter from the results (task 5436) and recommend where to spend.

team: Metrics reporting is the rung most at risk. Move juniors from 'pull the numbers' to 'explain the numbers'.
Have juniors write the experiment design before the content.
Re-check this role each data release; cracking rungs tend to break next.

project.title: Own a doc set, not a page
phases: Days 1–30: adopt the docs of an open-source project. Audit them: gaps, outdated pages, structure.

team: Juniors can still learn on editing work. Keep it, but require them to explain their edits.

project.title: Redesign one flow with real users
phases: Days 1–30: pick one painful flow (e.g. a government form). Run 5 user interviews and synthesise the findings.
Days 31–60: produce two concepts. Use AI for variations, and iterate on feedback (task 21694, only 20% automation).
Days 61–90: test the winner, document the technical constraints, and write the case study around the decisions.

team: Bug-fix design tickets are the at-risk rung. Don't build junior roles around them.
Put juniors in stakeholder reviews from the start; iterating on feedback is the most human-led rung in the data.
Use AI for exploring variations, and judge juniors on how they choose between them.
